Title: US Navy musician wins Sabah hearts with 'Original Sabahan' rendition
Article:
KOTA KINABALU: A US Navy musician has captured Sabahans' hearts after her rendition of the popular local song 'Original Sabahan' at the launch of Pacific Partnership 2026 (PP26) here two days ago went viral.
US Navy Musician 3rd Class Jasmine Rodriguez, 29, said her colleagues had described 'Original Sabahan' as Malaysia's version of 'Country Roads' because it was familiar to every generation and easy to sing along to.
"It's one of those songs that everyone knows and everyone can sing along to," she told the New Straits Times during the Pacific Partnership Band performance at a shopping mall here last night.
Netizens praised the 29-year-old from California for accurately singing the song by Atmosfera featuring Floor 88, which is in Bahasa Malaysia and Dusun.
Rodriguez was intrigued to learn during the interview that she had actually sung in two languages, rather than just Bahasa Malaysia, which she described as phonetic and easier to learn than Vietnamese.
During a previous mission, the vocalist also sang in different languages, including Tagalog and Indonesian, in other regions.
Prior to last night's performance, Rodriguez was surprised that some members of the public recognised her and took pictures with her.
"I am surprised that they could recognise me, probably because I am in the same uniform."
During the one-hour joint performance, the Pacific Partnership Band and Malaysian military band performed nine songs: 'Valerie', 'SESI Potret', 'Crazy In Love', 'Golden', 'Don't Stop Believing', 'Aku Penghibur', 'Budak Flat', 'Original Sabahan' and 'Unstoppable.'
The Pacific Partnership Band will also perform at various local schools, the Gaya Street Market concert on Sept 11, and the Pacific Partnership Fair on Sept 12.
Earlier in the day, some 460 members of the public benefited from free health education and basic healthcare information during a Community Health Engagement (CHE) organised by PP26 at the same venue.
The CHE gave the community an opportunity to meet military and civilian healthcare practitioners for free education on public health topics, including optometry, audiology, nutrition, dental care, physical therapy, rabies prevention, diabetes prevention, blood pressure, food safety, preventive medicine and more.

Title: Beneath the surface, peat fires keep burning
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The flames may be gone and the smoke may have subsided, but beneath the ground, a peat fire can continue burning.
This is among the challenges facing firefighters as the Fire and Rescue Department prepares for the possibility of severe fires flaring up in the country's forests should the current hot and dry spell persist.
Its director-general, Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohamad, said peat fires are particularly difficult to control because they spread beneath the surface and take considerably longer to extinguish than conventional bush fires.
The department is closely monitoring 62 locations nationwide, identified as being prone to large-scale forest fires exceeding 25ha.
They are among 183 locations identified as hotspots for open burning  based on records over the past five years.
Nor Hisham said the department was preparing for the potential impact of a Super El Nino developing in the Pacific that will peak in November.
Its effects are expected to be felt in Malaysia from the third or fourth week of January next year, with the northern and east coast states of Peninsular Malaysia, as well as Sabah among the areas of concern.
[[nid:1526593]]
Preparations are being strengthened through inter-agency cooperation, while high-risk areas will continue to be monitored to prevent fires from escalating.
For firefighters, some of the biggest challenges arise when fires break out in forests, peatlands and other remote locations that cannot be reached by their fire engines.
Portable pumps, hoses and firemen have to be transported into those areas using four-wheel-drive vehicles.
However, with modern technology, drones can be deployed to provide commanders with an aerial view of a fire.
"Drones help commanders assess the size of the affected area, identify the direction in which the fire is spreading and determine a more effective firefighting strategy," Nor Hisham said.
For major fires, personnel and equipment can be mobilised between stations, zones and states, while other agencies can be brought in to provide water sources, heavy machinery and logistical support.
Nor Hisham said the increasingly dry conditions meant prevention was just as important as firefighting.
Prolonged periods with little or no rainfall will dry out vegetation, making grass and bushes easier to ignite, while strong winds can turn a small fire into a rapidly spreading blaze.
The department has already recorded an increase in bush fires, from 1,199 last year to 1,815 so far this year.
Fires involving farms and plantations have also increased from 758 to 1,214.
Nor Hisham said humans were the main culprits, with many conducting open burning to dispose of rubbish and clear agricultural land. He urged the public not to underestimate small fires.
"Burning rubbish and garden waste, clearing agricultural land or burning other waste materials should be stopped because even a small fire can spread rapidly into bushes, forests and grassland," he added.

Title: US Embassy denies seeking to influence Malaysia's political leadership
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The United States Embassy in Kuala Lumpur has denied ever seeking to determine Malaysia's political leadership, calling any suggestion otherwise false.
In a statement, United States Chargé d'Affaires David H. Gamble Jr said Washington had never sought to decide Malaysia's political leadership.
The statement follows speculation online over the United States' alleged role in Malaysia's domestic political affairs.
The embassy has previously said its diplomatic engagement with Malaysia is focused on strengthening bilateral ties.

Title: Police probe alleged mistreatment of 2-year-old at Temerloh nursery
Article:
KUANTAN: Police are investigating the alleged mistreatment of a two-year-old girl by a nursery caretaker in Temerloh.
Temerloh police chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Nasyim Bahron said the girl's 29-year-old mother lodged a report about 6pm yesterday.
"An investigation paper has been opened, and the case is being investigated under Section 31(1) of the Child Act 2001," he said in a statement.
He said the completed investigation paper would be referred to the public prosecutor for further instructions.
The case has drawn widespread public attention after a video purportedly showing the girl being mistreated by the caretaker went viral on social media.

Title: Germany's far-right AfD seeks landmark state victory as Saxony-Anhalt votes
Article:
BERLIN, (Germany): Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls on Sunday in a closely watched election that could see the Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since the World War Two.
Under the smiling 35-year-old leader Ulrich Siegmund, the party has been polling comfortably ahead for months, and there is a genuine chance the AfD could take an absolute majority on Sunday evening, particularly if several smaller parties fail to clear Germany's five per cent threshold to enter parliament.
The vote is being closely watched as a barometer for the government of the deeply unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has attempted to chip away at the AfD's popularity by taking a tougher line on migration and security.
Recent surveys place the AfD at just over 40 per cent, followed by Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 per cent.
An absolute majority would allow the AfD to bypass mainstream parties' efforts to keep the party blocked out of power by refusing to work with it under a longstanding "firewall" policy.
Achieving an absolute majority is a high bar to clear in Germany's proportional electoral system, which was designed in part to encourage coalition governments and make it difficult for one party to rule alone.
If the AfD falls short of an outright majority, a CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome, though the exact shape of any coalition would depend on which parties enter.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow Sunday's vote.
AfD 'can no longer be stopped'
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt election is a stepping stone towards its larger ambitions of securing national power in the next federal election scheduled for 2029.
"No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund at a final rally on Saturday evening.
"Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt — what is currently sweeping across all of Germany — can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd in Saxony-Anhalt's capital, Magdeburg.
However, without an absolute majority, the AfD, which has been classified as "far-right extremist" by the state security service, would struggle to enter government due to the firewall.
Such a result opens the prospect of complex coalition negotiations, dependent on which parties can hit the five per cent hurdle.
Polls show one of the CDU's current coalition partners, the FDP, falling short, while the other, the SPD, is under 10 per cent.
The small far-left BSW, the only party that has not ruled out a coalition with the AfD, is also likely to miss out.
For Schulze, who is favoured in polls as voters' top choice for leader, combining with the SPD and Greens might not be enough for a majority, but the CDU has ruled out a coalition with the far-left Left Party that could help it reach that threshold.
One option could be a minority government led by Schulze that would depend on passive tolerance from the Left - a model used in the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia.
Initial results are expected around 6pm (1600 GMT) on Sunday evening shortly after polls close. — REUTERS

Title: Argentina threatens to sanction oil projects around Falklands
Article:
BUENOS AIRES: Argentina has announced that it will investigate and sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands without authorisation, after President Javier Milei said the "winds of change" favour his country's claim to the archipelago.
Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, a British overseas territory that Argentines call Las Malvinas.
Argentina's presidency said in a statement Friday that it had ordered proceedings to "investigate and penalise" 45 entities "linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons" around the Falklands.
The statement did not name the entities involved. According to Argentine media, they include British, US, Canadian, Israeli, Danish and Dutch companies.
On Saturday afternoon, oilfield services companies Schlumberger, Halliburton and Baker Hughes issued statements saying they do not and will not work on hydrocarbon projects near the islands.
Later, Milei shared a news item on X reporting the statements, along with an acronym that translates to "everything is going according to plan".
The Falklands are located about 600 kilometres east of Argentina's southernmost tip and administered by Britain. The Falklands War in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentine government after 74 days of conflict that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops.
In a speech Thursday, Milei renewed claims to the Falklands and announced tougher sanctions on companies linked to oil projects nearby.
"There are winds of change in the world that are favourable to our claim," Milei said.
Milei's speech followed comments from US President Donald Trump on Monday that the United States was reviewing its position on the Falkland Islands.
According to media reports, Washington has threatened to oppose Britain's sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago if it does not increase its Nato defence spending.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting responded by asserting Britain's "unshakeable" commitment to the Falklands.
"The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British," he said in a social media post Friday.

Title: Century-old Penang coffee shop to close [WATCH]
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: A 106-year-old Hainanese coffee shop will close on Sept 26 as no family member is willing to carry its three-generation legacy into the future.
Kong Thai Lai, a fixture of Penang's traditional coffee shop scene, will serve its final cup at its Lebuh Dickens premises here after the landlord decided to take back the property.
For third-generation operator Tan Jeng Seow, 68, the closure is not merely the end of a tenancy, but the end of a family business.
"Nowadays, youngsters don't tend to do business like a coffee shop. They have their own interests and priorities, so perhaps the legacy is not for them," he told the
New Straits Times
during an interview at his shop here recently.
Tan, who has run the business for 14 years, said his son, who works overseas, is not interested in taking over.
His nieces and nephews are also working and have shown no interest in continuing the business.
"If they were interested, they would have called me to say, 'Hey, we're going to close. I'm going to do it', right? But there has been no response from them."
Tan himself never intended to take over the family business. After working at a takeaway shop in London, he returned to Penang, where his brother was running the coffee shop.
When his brother died, Tan stepped in and continued the business, keeping the family legacy alive for another 14 years.
Now, however, there is no one in the next generation prepared to do the same.
The business was founded by Tan's grandfather in 1920 in Lorong Hutton, where the family operated for about 80 years.
It later moved to Lebuh Leith, before settling in Lebuh Dickens in 2022.
Tan said the repeated relocations were costly and exhausting, and he was unwilling to start over again at another location.
"It's quite a hassle to move. When you move, you have to start all over again."
Although loyal customers have urged him to continue elsewhere, some even helping to look for vacant premises, Tan said he had decided it was time to stop.
"I think I've had enough. I'm quite exhausted. I'm so tired, so I am looking forward to a good rest."
Kong Thai Lai is known for its traditional coffee blend, homemade kaya, and butter and kaya toast.
Its clientele has included generations of local families as well as visitors from China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
The coffee shop also holds a place in Penang's business history.
The late tycoon Tan Sri Loh Boon Siew was a regular and reportedly once offered RM10,000 for his favourite marble-top table, but the family declined to part with it.
Business magnate Tan Sri Robert Kuok was also a customer and was said to have bought the shop's coffee powder after enjoying its brew.
Tan said the family would retain the coffee shop's name and some of its old furnishings and memorabilia.
But whether the business itself survives remains uncertain.
After more than a century, the family legacy may end not because customers stopped coming, but because there is simply no one left in the family willing to carry it forward.
Tan's message was simple: "Thank you for the support all these years. I really appreciate it."

Title: Ronald Stephen McCoy: Enduring legacy of courage, compassion and hope
Article:
DATUK Dr Ronald Stephen McCoy, the renowned Malaysian obstetrician and gynaecologist, physician, humanitarian and lifelong campaigner for nuclear disarmament, passed away on Sept 1, 2026 at the age of 96.
With his passing, Malaysia lost an extraordinary doctor whose lifelong career was dedicated to two seemingly different causes — the noble calling of bringing new life into the world and advocating for the global struggle against the catastrophic consequences of nuclear war.
Born in Seremban in 1930, McCoy was educated at Victoria Institution in Kuala Lumpur, where he distinguished himself not only academically but also on the sporting field. He later entered the University of Malaya in Singapore in 1949 as part of its first intake of medical students.
Medicine became his life's vocation. He trained in obstetrics and gynaecology and went on to serve at Kuala Lumpur General Hospital, Assunta Hospital and Pantai Medical Centre, becoming one of the founding members of Pantai Medical Centre.
Over approximately four decades of medical practice, he delivered 20,000 babies — an extraordinary legacy measured not in statistics alone, but in the thousands of Malaysian families whose lives he touched with the miracle of birth. He retired from clinical practice in 1996.
However, McCoy's conception of a doctor's responsibility was far reaching. His experiences during the Second World War, and particularly his reflections on the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, left him deeply concerned about the destructive effects of nuclear weapons.
He believed that doctors had a special mission to warn humanity about a catastrophe for which medicine could offer no adequate response.
In 1987, he founded the Malaysian Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War, linking Malaysian doctors to the international movement against nuclear weapons.
He subsequently became vice-president of the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW) for the Asia-Pacific region and served as its co-president for eight years.
IPPNW had itself been awarded the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize for its efforts to raise awareness of the medical consequences of nuclear war.
McCoy's most enduring contribution to the global peace movement, however, came after the failure of the 2005 review of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Frustrated by the lack of progress, he proposed a new international grassroots campaign modelled on the successful campaign against landmines. He suggested the name International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN).
The idea was subsequently developed into a worldwide movement. Launched in 2007, ICAN grew into a coalition of hundreds of organisations campaigning for a legally binding prohibition of nuclear weapons.
In 2017, its extraordinary efforts were recognised when ICAN was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
For McCoy, however, the campaign was never about personal recognition. It was about the future of humanity — particularly the future of children, some of whom he had helped bring into the world.
He often connected his anti-nuclear activism to his work as an obstetrician, arguing that the thousands of babies he had delivered deserved to grow up in a world free from the threat of nuclear annihilation.
His contribution to public life certainly extended beyond medicine and nuclear disarmament.
He served as president of the Malaysian Medical Association and participated in Malaysia's delegation to the International Court of Justice in 1995 during its consideration of the legal status of nuclear weapons.
He was also a member of the Canberra Commission on the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
McCoy's legacy is undoubtedly profound. He was a Malaysian who carried his country's voice onto the international stage, a peace activist who refused to accept nuclear annihilation as an inevitable part of humanity's future.
Twenty thousand babies entered the world through his hands. His life's work was to ensure that they, and the generations that followed them, would inherit a world worthy of them.
McCoy leaves behind a legacy of courage and compassion. He is survived by children Stephen, David and Ruth and grandchildren Lara, Miraya, Sacha and Hannah. May he rest in peace.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Two dead, 14 missing after Bolivia army base blasts
Article:
VIACHA, (Bolivia): At least 14 soldiers remained missing after two explosions at a military base in Bolivia killed two and injured more than 80, the base commander said Saturday.
The blasts occurred Friday afternoon at a facility where explosives are stored in the town of Viacha, home to about 114,000 people and located 30 kilometres (18 miles) southwest of La Paz.
Streets in the area remained littered with rubble on Saturday, while windows in nearby buildings were shattered.
"Fourteen uniformed personnel who were in the area affected by the two explosions at the Viacha military base have not yet been located," base commander Colonel Antonio Amaru said in a statement, adding that search and rescue efforts were underway.
The Ministry of Defence identified the missing as a sergeant and 13 conscripts, aged 18 and 19.
The dead were two young men who had been serving their first year of mandatory military service.
The cause of the blasts, which sent a plume of smoke into the air, was under investigation.
Distraught relatives confronted police officers with riot shields who were blocking access to the base.
Some indigenous Aymara people tearfully asked soldiers about their loved ones, while others tried in vain to force their way in, an AFP reporter saw.
"They haven't moved even a single stone, not even a bit of cement, they haven't moved anything. My nephew is still inside the rubble," Adolfo Copa told AFP.
Irineo Mamani, 65, said he just wanted to confirm if his son was on the list of missing persons.
"We just want them to tell us if a certain soldier is there, and that's all," he said.
'Shockwave'
The force of the blasts tore off roofs, sent rocks flying and uprooted trees, affecting dozens of nearby homes.
In a report Friday, Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said the first explosion involved "black powder, corresponding to pyrotechnic material stored at the site", while the cause of the second, larger explosion was being analysed.
The second explosion "blew me five metres backward," a neighbourhood resident with facial injuries told the newspaper El Deber, adding that he had lost consciousness.
President Rodrigo Paz on Friday expressed "deep solidarity with the families of the deceased, the injured and all residents affected by the explosions".
He said he had ordered a "thorough, technical and transparent" investigation.
"We must establish with absolute clarity the causes of this event, verify compliance with safety protocols and determine any responsibilities that may arise," he said in a post on X.
Authorities in Viacha declared three days of mourning, while the town's public prosecutor's office said Saturday it had opened an investigation into manslaughter and other crimes.

Title: Tens of thousands of Croatians protest over hazardous waste
Article:
ZAGREB: Tens of thousands of people rallied in Zagreb on Saturday seeking the immediate cleanup of thousands of tonnes of illegally dumped hazardous waste in one of Croatia's most pristine areas.
Some 35,000 tonnes of waste, including electronic and medical waste, were found in early 2025 in the Lika region, known for its pristine forests and rivers and home to national parks and the country's longest mountain range.
Authorities have been investigating 10 people and four companies over the dumping. They are suspected of importing waste from Slovenia, Italy and Germany and illegally dumping or burying it alongside medical waste from Croatia in Gospic, in the pristine region.
In August, prosecutors published a report confirming soil contamination in Gospic, adding that the waste, which had spread beyond the dumping site, presented a "significant risk for the environment and people's health", though drinking water in Gospic remained safe, according to health authorities.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets of central Zagreb in a march dubbed "Walk for Lika, Walk for Croatia", backed by President Zoran Milanovic, the opposition, and numerous public figures and non-government organisations.
"I want a beautiful, clean and healthy Croatia for my children, that they can drink water from any tap in this country," Katarina Kenda, who joined the march with her three children, told AFP.
"This is a very serious incident and it must be stopped now, before the whole of Croatia ends up buried in waste."
"Ecocide equals slow genocide" and "Halt waste import", read some of the banners carried by the protesters, many of whom waved Croatian flags.
Organisers demanded that the authorities present a concrete cleanup plan within the next 20 days, remove the waste within the next three months, and hold those responsible accountable.
Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said earlier this month that the site would be covered by mid-October and the removal would follow.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Putin holds Ukraine talks with US envoys
Article:
MOSCOW: Russian leader Vladimir Putin held around three hours of late-night talks in the Kremlin with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on ending more than four years of war with Ukraine on Saturday, ahead of their first visit to Kyiv on Sunday.
US President Donald Trump has said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing a "proposal" on ending the fighting.
Talks ended after just over three hours, past 11pm in Moscow.
The envoys are due on Sunday in Ukraine's capital for the first time, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe's worst conflict since World War Two.
Both Russia and Ukraine agreed not to strike each other's capitals for three days to allow the negotiations to take place.
In televised comments before the closed-door talks began, Putin thanked Trump for "not stopping" to try to end the war — launched by Russia in 2022 — despite it being "not simple".
The Russian leader has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine and Washington did not say if its plan involves Kyiv ceding land.
The envoys arrived after a summer of escalation that saw a drastic rise in civilian deaths on both sides. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and forced millions of people to flee their homes.
Kyiv said Saturday that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country — including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv.
Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv — a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war.
"We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves," Putin told Witkoff and Kushner.
Limited truce
Putin was speaking a day after Kyiv said Moscow had struck the headquarters of its SBU security service in the centre of the city.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have said they would halt strikes on each other's cities to allow for negotiations.
"The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy — who had offered a truce during the US visits — later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow," Zelenskyy said on social media.
On Saturday, Putin said he had "noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced" its strikes on Russia and Moscow.
Putin also said he had been informed the two US envoys would be heading to Kyiv — their first time for talks in the Ukrainian capital.
"In any case, of course, no matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial," he added.
Zelenskyy has said he expects the US envoys in Kyiv Sunday.
US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war — which has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
As peace efforts stalled, in part because of Washington's war with Iran, Moscow and Kyiv stepped up their long-range attacks.
Russian strikes
As the US envoys were in the Kremlin, Ukraine said Russian attacks had killed three members of the same family in the city of Chuhuiv in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
"As a result of this shelling, almost the entire family was killed: A 19-year-old girl, an 11-year-old boy, and a 45-year-old man," regional leader Oleg Synegubov said.
Earlier Saturday, Russia struck Kyiv's suburbs and in the Dnipro region, where local officials said five people had been killed.
Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to disrupt the visit of the US envoys with overnight attacks on Kyiv's two airports — as well as on civilian targets.
This will be the first time that Witkoff and Kushner visit Kyiv since Trump returned to office last year with a pledge to resolve the conflict.
Travelling to Kyiv by plane would be a highly unusual move, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 because of the war. Visiting leaders and officials have generally travelled there by train.
Witkoff and Kushner, who have been involved in negotiations for ceasefires in Gaza and Iran, have travelled repeatedly to Moscow in previous attempts at diplomacy.
Their visit comes after a rare trip to Moscow last month by CIA director John Ratcliffe.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Negligence is all it takes to spark huge fire, warns Fire Dept
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A carelessly discarded cigarette butt, an unattended pile of burning rubbish or a small fire used to clear land is all it takes to ignite a major bush or peat fire during the current hot and dry spell.
Fire and Rescue Department director-general Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohamad said prolonged dry weather had stripped moisture from grass, bushes and other vegetation, effectively providing ready fuel for fires.
He said hot weather was not necessarily the cause of major fires, but could turn even a minor ignition source into a major blaze.
[[nid:1526600]]
Nor Hisham said strong winds could spread flames through dry vegetation, widening the area firefighters must contain.
The warning comes following a sharp rise in open-burning incidents nationwide during the recent hot and dry spell.
Cases climbed from 53 on Aug 20 to 70 the following day before jumping to 180 on Aug 22 and peaking at 231 on Aug 23. Another 190 incidents were recorded on Aug 24.
Nor Hisham said the figures highlighted the importance of preventing fires from starting in the first place, particularly as prolonged periods of little or no rainfall continued to dry out vegetation.
Bush and grass fires account for the bulk of such incidents, with 18,426 recorded nationwide so far this year.
[[nid:1526599]]
He said people should avoid burning rubbish and garden waste as well as using fire to clear agricultural land during the current conditions.
Fires should never be left unattended and smokers should ensure cigarette butts are completely extinguished and disposed of properly.
"Even a small fire can spread rapidly into bushes, forests and land," he added.
Nor Hisham said open burning is an offence under Section 29A of the Environmental Quality Act 1974, with enforcement and prosecution under the jurisdiction of the Department of Environment.
He said the Fire and Rescue Department would share information with other enforcement agencies if evidence of open burning was detected during firefighting operations.
[[nid:1526598]]

Title: US, Iranian forces fire at vessels in waters near Iran
Article:
DUBAI: US and Iranian forces fired at vessels in waters around Iran on Saturday, including three Iranian oil carriers struck by the Americans and three tankers that Iran said it targeted while on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
US Central Command said it struck the three Iranian vessels, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near Iran's oil export hub, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours," said Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, which oversees the US military in the Middle East.
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region, and said later it targeted the three tankers as well as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
"Do not be deceived by the 'terrorist' US military and refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at passing through unauthorised waterways," the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried on Iranian state TV. "Otherwise, you will be targeted."
Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news agency, had reported that four US missiles hit a tanker in the area of Kharg's anchorage. Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker's crew was being evacuated.
No American personnel were harmed, Central Command said.
The exchange of attacks followed an escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has continued since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from a majority of Americans before congressional elections in November.
[[nid:1526583]]
TRUMP'S THREATS OVER KHARG ISLAND
While US President Donald Trump's administration seeks to pivot towards an economic clampdown on Iran by widening sanctions, the president himself has kept open the possibility of military action.
On Aug 31, Trump issued a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video depicting Kharg Island being "blown to smithereens". Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90 per cent of its crude via Kharg Island before the war. Flows have been disrupted since a US blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
Trump has spoken of an attack on Kharg before. He said on June 11 that he wanted to take over the island, but then said a US military operation there was off the table, days before Tehran and Washington signed an interim agreement aimed at ending the war on June 17.
A US attack on Kharg would further pressure Iran's oil industry and its wider economy, which is already reeling from the US naval blockade.
The US imposed its blockade on Iranian ports after Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, an important waterway that carried one-fifth of the world's oil supply before the war.
Brent crude futures closed at their highest level since July 24 on Friday, at US$96.28 a barrel, as tensions in the Middle East drive global supply concerns.

Title: Beneath the surface, peat fires keep burning
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The flames may be gone and the smoke may have subsided, but beneath the ground, a peat fire can continue burning.
This is among the challenges facing firefighters as the Fire and Rescue Department prepares for the possibility of severe fires flaring up in the country's forests should the current hot and dry spell persist.
Its director-general, Datuk Seri Nor Hisham Mohamad, said peat fires are particularly difficult to control because they spread beneath the surface and take considerably longer to extinguish than conventional bush fires.
The department is closely monitoring 62 locations nationwide, identified as being prone to large-scale forest fires exceeding 25ha.
They are among 183 locations identified as hotspots for open burning  based on records over the past five years.
Nor Hisham said the department was preparing for the potential impact of a Super El Nino developing in the Pacific that will peak in November.
Its effects are expected to be felt in Malaysia from the third or fourth week of January next year, with the northern and east coast states of Peninsular Malaysia, as well as Sabah among the areas of concern.
[[nid:1526590]]
Preparations are being strengthened through inter-agency cooperation, while high-risk areas will continue to be monitored to prevent fires from escalating.
For firefighters, some of the biggest challenges arise when fires break out in forests, peatlands and other remote locations that cannot be reached by their fire engines.
Portable pumps, hoses and firemen have to be transported into those areas using four-wheel-drive vehicles.
However, with modern technology, drones can be deployed to provide commanders with an aerial view of a fire.
"Drones help commanders assess the size of the affected area, identify the direction in which the fire is spreading and determine a more effective firefighting strategy," Nor Hisham said.
For major fires, personnel and equipment can be mobilised between stations, zones and states, while other agencies can be brought in to provide water sources, heavy machinery and logistical support.
Nor Hisham said the increasingly dry conditions meant prevention was just as important as firefighting.
Prolonged periods with little or no rainfall will dry out vegetation, making grass and bushes easier to ignite, while strong winds can turn a small fire into a rapidly spreading blaze.
The department has already recorded an increase in bush fires, from 1,199 last year to 1,815 so far this year.
Fires involving farms and plantations have also increased from 758 to 1,214.
Nor Hisham said humans were the main culprits, with many conducting open burning to dispose of rubbish and clear agricultural land. He urged the public not to underestimate small fires.
"Burning rubbish and garden waste, clearing agricultural land or burning other waste materials should be stopped because even a small fire can spread rapidly into bushes, forests and grassland," he added.

Title: Venezuelan billionaire once probed by US now has Pentagon oil deal
Article:
CARACAS/MIAMI: The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration's sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was until recently a target of US money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA.
Now, after assisting US authorities ahead of the capture of authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro, Alejandro Betancourt is Washington's key partner in an unusual oil agreement with Caracas.
According to last week's announcement, the US gains access to about one-fifth of Venezuela's crude reserves for decades. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35 per cent stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Betancourt's company and a known crude producer in Venezuela. The State Department gets the right to buy 20 per cent of NABEP's oil at cost, and preferential access to the remaining 80 per cent of output.
The deal marks a striking change of fortune for Betancourt, who four people familiar with US policy in Venezuela said was key to US strategy and planning in the lead-up to the Jan 3 operation that removed former President Maduro from power and flew him to New York to face charges of drug trafficking, which Maduro denies.
Asked about the investigations of Betancourt, a US official who declined to be named said most of the legal challenges were nearly a decade old — and that he currently has no legal problems in the US. NABEP's record of pumping oil in Venezuela made Betancourt the best partner to help boost output under the arrangement, the official said.
Reuters could not determine precisely when US federal prosecutors paused their investigation into Betancourt or whether it came in exchange for his cooperation with the Trump administration.
Sarah Chouraqui, NABEP's lawyer, said Betancourt had a strong record of operating in complex energy markets. "The allegations in question have been examined extensively by authorities in multiple jurisdictions, and no charges have been brought against him," she said in an email.
Chouraqui did not address questions about his assistance to the Trump administration or his legal cases.
INFORMATION THAT HELPED ENFORCE US BLOCKADE
In the months before Maduro's capture, the billionaire provided information that helped enforce a US naval blockade targeting sanctioned oil tankers operating in Venezuela, which led to the seizure or interdiction of more than a dozen vessels, according to the four people who spoke on condition of anonymity. He also facilitated negotiations with officials including Delcy Rodriguez, who became interim president after Maduro's capture.
The Venezuelan government did not respond to requests for comment.
After Maduro's removal, Betancourt's role as a key intermediary continued, helping broker oil deals and other partnerships and continuing to assist communications between Washington and Caracas to kickstart Venezuela's economy, according to seven sources.
In January, Betancourt helped broker a key oil trading agreement that has led to the export of more than 135 million barrels of crude and fuel to the US, Europe, India and the Caribbean so far, according to vessel monitoring data and six people with knowledge of the negotiations. That's about half of all oil exports through the end of August.
Reuters could not determine his exact role in the discussions.
Betancourt has also popped in on meetings at Venezuela's Miraflores presidential palace, according to two people familiar with the matter. He was also at Miraflores during this week's visit by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Wright told reporters, though Betancourt did not appear with Wright and Rodriguez at a signing ceremony for oil deals.
Betancourt has been investigated in the US, Spain and Switzerland but never indicted.
Earlier this year US federal prosecutors in Florida paused their investigation into Betancourt in connection with an alleged plan that involved embezzling over $1 billion from Venezuela's state-owned oil company and laundering it through real estate in Miami and bank accounts in Malta and Switzerland.
Two of those people said US prosecutors had been subsequently discouraged by supervisors from investigating Betancourt further.
Prosecutors on the case were not given a rationale, four people familiar with the case said.
After the investigation stalled, US officials pressured the Swiss government to ease its inquiries into the tycoon, said four people familiar with the matter. Switzerland, which was also investigating Betancourt for money laundering, dropped its request to extradite him from the United Kingdom in May, said the sources.
The Zurich Public Prosecutor's Office declined to comment on whether the US influenced the decision to withdraw its extradition request, but said the case against Betancourt was still proceeding.
"The extradition request was withdrawn because of particular aspects of UK extradition law, which we cannot discuss in detail," the Office said. "This step concerns only the extradition proceedings in the UK. The criminal proceedings against the accused are otherwise unaffected and will continue."
The withdrawal was unusual, said Mark Pieth, a Swiss legal scholar and anti-corruption expert. "You would not do that if the case is continuing," he said.
The United Kingdom's Home Office declined to comment.
A YOUNG GENERATION OF BUSINESS LEADERS
Betancourt is a prominent member of the so-called Bolichicos — a younger generation of business people who amassed fortunes during the administration of former Venezuelan leader Hugo Chavez. His company Derwick Associates won roughly US$2 billion in government contracts to build power plants during the country's electricity crisis in the 2010s — some without competitive bidding — despite having little construction experience.
Government data later showed many of the plants operated at a fraction of their intended capacity or not at all, as Venezuela's power grid continued to suffer widespread blackouts. Betancourt and Derwick have repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said the facilities were completed and that later failures resulted from mismanagement by state authorities. Rodriguez told a press conference on Wednesday that all legal proceedings against Betancourt's companies in Venezuela were dismissed years ago.
In 2012, Betancourt entered into a partnership with state-controlled company PDVSA to operate mature fields in western Venezuela. These would eventually become the core production of NABEP, which Betancourt co-founded with Florida billionaire Harry Sargeant in April 2024. Sargeant sold his shares in NABEP last month.
Mauricio Claver-Carone, a Miami businessman and former Trump administration adviser who implemented US policy in Caracas in an unofficial role, told Reuters last month that Betancourt is a useful intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodriguez because he understands the oil business in both countries. He added that Betancourt had been helpful to the first Trump administration.
But several former US intelligence officials, prosecutors and diplomats privately expressed concern regarding Betancourt's influence on US policy, because of the previous investigation in the US and ongoing investigation in Switzerland, as well as his proximity to high-ranking officials from the former Hugo Chavez and Maduro governments.
Federal prosecutors are "scratching their heads," said one former prosecutor with knowledge of the situation.
Before the Miami-based investigation into Betancourt was put on hold, six sources said he had been identified as an unnamed unindicted co-conspirator in an alleged plan by former Venezuelan energy officials and their associates to launder more than $1 billion misappropriated from the state-owned PDVSA oil company. Ten people have been indicted since 2018.
In Spain, authorities launched a new investigation into Betancourt for money laundering last year involving US$4 billion allegedly embezzled from PDVSA, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.
Reuters was unable to determine if he remained under investigation.
Spain's National Court and the Venezuelan state oil company did not respond to requests for comment.
Once he was free to leave the UK, Betancourt travelled to Venezuela in late June and again in July, both times departing from West Palm Beach, Florida, according to flight manifests seen by Reuters.
Betancourt's lawyer Chouraqui did not comment on his travel.

Title: Malaysia's Taanusiya Chetty wins second runner-up at Miss World 2026
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Teacher and activist Taanusiya Chetty has been crowned the second runner-up at the 2026 Miss World pageant, which was held in Vietnam today.
The 26-year-old represented Malaysia in the 73rd edition of the pageant.
The iconic sapphire-studded crown went to Joheirry Mola of the Dominican Republic, who was crowned Miss World this year.
Elisabeth Reynes of Spain was named the first runner-up.
A total of 111 contestants from around the world took part in the pageant, which was held in Nha Trang.
As the pageant progressed, the field was narrowed to the Top 40, followed by the Top 20, and Top 12, before being reduced to the Top 6.
The six finalists then faced a question-and-answer round with the judges, who decided which contestant would be crowned the new Miss World.
Many social media users took to their respective accounts to praise Taanusiya, not only for her beauty but also for her presence and confidence as she commanded the stage during the question-and-answer session.
"I would influence students to plant trees at a very young age. Because that is also a responsibility for them to understand how a plant can take time to grow from the seeds they planted.
"And imagine walking on a path full of thunderstorms, and you don't have anyone to offer you an umbrella.
"But I want to be that sort of teacher who offers the students, no matter what background they are from, the seeds they planted take time to grow.
"And when you do that, you will influence many other people around the world," Taanusiya said when asked, "What responsibility do you have to protect the environment for future generations, and how would you inspire children to join that mission?" during the question-and-answer round.

Title: Dismantle the corruption 'gravy train' to end systemic corruption
Article:
THE NST editorial by Sharanjit Singh, "The rot has to stop: Time to end the plunder of the gravy train," is timely and deserves serious public attention.
Its significance extends beyond the individual corruption cases currently before the courts.
From a criminological perspective, the more fundamental concern is whether corruption has become sufficiently embedded within Malaysia's political, administrative and economic structures to reproduce itself despite investigations, prosecutions and convictions.
The editorial's call to end the "gravy train" should therefore be understood not simply as a moral appeal, but as a call for structural reform.
Corruption becomes particularly dangerous when access to public office, public resources and political influence creates opportunities for private enrichment.
The criminological problem is consequently not merely dishonest individuals but institutional environments in which corruption can become rational, profitable and eventually normalised.
Criminology teaches us that crime is facilitated by opportunity. Where there is substantial discretion, large sums of public money, inadequate transparency, weak oversight and limited accountability, opportunities for corruption increase.
Public procurement, government-linked entities, major infrastructure projects, licensing, concessions and politically connected businesses should therefore be regarded as potential crime-risk environments, requiring systematic prevention rather than simply post-offence investigation.
This raises an important question: why are opportunities for corruption allowed to arise in the first place? Prosecution is necessary but it is fundamentally reactive.
By the time a corruption case reaches court, public money may already have been lost, institutions damaged and public confidence weakened.
Malaysia therefore needs to move from a predominantly case-driven anti-corruption strategy towards a risk-based criminological approach that identifies vulnerabilities before misconduct occurs.
Public procurement deserves particular attention because it involves substantial public expenditure and complex decision-making.
The emphasis should be on preventing corruption at the design and decision-making stages, rather than relying predominantly on investigations after funds have disappeared.
Independent oversight, transparent tender processes, effective conflict-of-interest declarations and systematic audits should become integral components of corruption prevention.
Another issue requiring greater emphasis is that corruption is rarely a one-person crime. Sophisticated corruption can involve networks connecting politicians, public officials, intermediaries, companies, contractors and professional facilitators.
Investigating only the individual who receives an illicit benefit may therefore leave the wider network intact. A criminological approach must examine the entire criminal ecosystem, who creates the opportunity, who facilitates it, who finances it and who ultimately benefits.
Closely related is the issue of beneficial ownership. The person receiving a government contract or controlling a company may not necessarily be the ultimate beneficiary.
Corporate structures, nominees and intermediaries can potentially obscure financial interests. Consequently, greater transparency is required concerning who ultimately owns and benefits from companies receiving significant public contracts.
A further issue insufficiently addressed in many corruption debates is political financing. Opaque political funding can create relationships of obligation between donors, political actors and businesses.
[[nid:1526487]]
This creates the potential for patronage, preferential treatment and policy capture. Malaysia therefore requires a comprehensive political-financing framework with meaningful disclosure requirements, clear limits and independent oversight.
Institutional independence is equally critical. Anti-corruption agencies, prosecutors, auditors and regulatory bodies must not merely possess legal powers; they must have sufficient independence and public credibility to exercise those powers without fear or favour.
Public confidence in the criminal justice response is itself an important component of deterrence.
Indeed, deterrence should not be measured simply by the severity of punishment. For sophisticated white-collar offenders, the certainty of detection may be more significant than the severity of punishment.
If individuals believe that the likelihood of detection is remote, substantial potential rewards may continue to outweigh perceived risks.
Malaysia consequently needs stronger financial intelligence, proactive auditing, data-driven monitoring and closer scrutiny of high-risk transactions.
Whistleblower protection is another critical but often under appreciated component of corruption prevention. Employees and insiders may be the first to recognise irregularities, conflicts of interest or manipulation.
If they fear retaliation or professional consequences, silence becomes the rational response. Effective whistleblower mechanisms must therefore provide genuine protection, confidentiality and confidence that complaints will be independently investigated.
Perhaps the most difficult problem is the normalisation of corruption. When patronage, preferential treatment, political connections or the misuse of public resources are perceived as simply "the way things work", corruption ceases to appear exceptional.
This represents a dangerous cultural shift. The objective must therefore be not merely to punish corrupt behaviour but to change the institutional and social environment that makes such behaviour tolerable.
Malaysia's recent improvement in international corruption perceptions is encouraging, but it should not become a reason for complacency.
Progress in perception indicators is valuable but it does not by itself demonstrate that structural corruption risks have been eliminated.
What matters ultimately is whether institutions become more transparent, accountable and resistant to abuse.
The NST editorial should therefore be regarded as a warning as much as a call to action. Ending the "gravy train" requires more than waiting for the next scandal to emerge.
Malaysia needs a comprehensive National Corruption Prevention Framework based on criminological risk assessment.
High-risk ministries, agencies, government-linked entities and major projects should undergo systematic corruption-risk assessments, with independent scrutiny built into the process before public funds are committed.
Ultimately, corruption is not merely a criminal-justice problem. It is a problem of governance, institutional design, organisational culture and public trust.
The real measure of success is therefore not how many corrupt individuals are arrested or convicted.
It is whether Malaysia progressively eliminates the opportunities, incentives and institutional weaknesses that allow corruption to flourish.
The gravy train will finally stop not when the next offender is prosecuted but when the tracks that allow the train to run are dismantled.
* The writer is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research, Universiti Sains Malaysia

Title: Haze shuts 63 schools in Bintulu, Tatau and Sebauh
Article:
KUCHING: A total of 63 schools in Bintulu, Tatau and Sebauh will be closed from Sept 7 to 11 after the air pollutant index (API) reading in Bintulu reached the "very unhealthy" level.
The Sarawak Education Department (JPNS) said the temporary closure involved 54 primary schools with 22,476 students and nine secondary schools with 17,268 students under the Bintulu and Tatau/Sebauh District Education Offices (PPDs).
The decision was made based on continuous monitoring and API readings reaching the "very unhealthy" level at 8pm today.
According to the Department of Environment's (DOE) Malaysian air pollutant index management system (APIMS), Bintulu recorded an API reading of 206 at 8pm today.
In a statement tonight, JPNS said Home-Based Teaching and Learning (PdPR) would be implemented throughout the closure period.
The department said any changes or latest information would be announced from time to time.
It also reminded schools to comply with the prescribed standard operating procedures and prioritise the health of students and teachers.
Educational institutions were also advised to refer to APIMS for the latest API readings in their respective areas or districts and comply with recommendations issued by the Health Ministry to safeguard the health of students and education personnel.
With the latest closures, a total of 617 primary schools involving 130,953 students and 93 secondary schools involving 107,350 students under 14 PPDs affected by cross-border haze in Sarawak have been temporarily closed.

Title: NST Leader: Were 'foxes' in charge of Tabung Haji?
Article:
TABUNG HAJI is cash-rich, but as the Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) found out, it was governance-poor.
Reading the RCI report and subsequent investigations by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC), we reach an inevitable conclusion: foxes were allegedly put in charge of the henhouse.
Little wonder then that Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim is supporting  tighter oversight of Tabung Haji, saying the measure is necessary to prevent abuse of power and other irregularities in the fund's management.
The RCI report covers the period between 2014 and 2020. Tighter oversight plus legal support have been long overdue.
Institutions entrusted with enormous responsibility have let people down over and over again.
Plug one hole, another pops up elsewhere, giving the impression that officers of integrity are very few. Is our talent pool a duck pond? It sure seems so given the repeated occurrence of such crimes.
We need to get things back on track fast. A few things must happen. First, Tabung Haji needs a more robust integrity system that goes beyond issuing policies and getting certificates to say everything is fine and dandy.
What it needs is to make integrity part of its structure. Tabung Haji is too important an institution to be left to compliance guidelines.
It must do the right thing even when no one is looking. A metaphorical CCTV system, you can say. This must be hard to circumvent. And then there is a very Malaysian malady: political interference. What has happened to the Federal Land Development Authority  over and over again is an example of a bad case of abuse of power and corruption.
In this game of political hide-and-seek, the powerless settlers always lose — we do not know how much they lost — but its former chairman, Tan Sri Isa Abdul Samad, was jailed for corruption involving RM3.09 million.
Imagine, Isa was a menteri besar of Negri Sembilan. How could he fall so low? We have to blame political interference that keeps independent investigation at bay as long as possible. 1Malaysia Development Bhd is a classic display of this.
An attorney-general lost his job when he was about to give instructions to the MACC to investigate Datuk Seri Najib Razak. A few MACC officers were affected, too.
Second, Putrajaya must ensure no politician holds any power in institutions which have enormous responsibility.
Tabung Haji is certainly one. We need a professional board and management. Many seem to be there just for money.
Settlers need their investments in the land to grow, but by some peculiar human resource management process, the top team seems to be interested in anything but. Finally, accountability.
The power that be thinks this to be least important. In fact, where accountability is absent, impunity takes the institutions further downhill.

Title: Haze forces last-minute cancellation of PJ Half Marathon
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Petaling Jaya Half Marathon, which was expected to draw 10,000 participants tomorrow, has been cancelled due to the haze.
In a post on the PJ Half Marathon's Facebook page about two hours ago, the organisers said the decision was made after taking into consideration the Air Pollutant Index readings, as well as the health and well-being of the runners.
"While the latest forecast indicates that the Air Pollutant Index may improve over the next 24 hours, the reading remains within the unhealthy range, which may have an impact on the health and well-being of our runners, volunteers, crew and everyone involved in the event.
"As runners, the safety of our running community must come first.
"After careful consideration, we believe that cancelling the event is the wisest and most responsible decision we can make at this time," the statement said.
However, the statement said registered runners who still wished to run tomorrow would be able to take part in a 5km route as an optional alternative.
Petaling Jaya Mayor Datuk Mohd Yazid Sairi had said last month that the event would also feature international runners from 34 countries.
Yazid had also said at the time that about 9,000 participants had registered for the marathon.
The event was scheduled to feature five categories, namely the 30km, 21km, 10km, 5km fun run and 1km costume-themed fun run.
The first race was scheduled to start at Laman MBPJ in Petaling Jaya about 3.30am.

Title: Grief on Chinese Internet as wait for Tibet flood news drags on
Article:
PHOTOS of sons, daughters, uncles and husbands pepper Chinese social media, shared by people hoping for news about relatives missing since deadly floods on the border with Nepal on Aug 26.
Hundreds of people remain unaccounted for on the Tibetan side of the frontier, where Chinese authorities keep tight control over media access and sources of information.
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities have given regular updates on the rising number of dead and display names of the missing, while national media show images of families  grieving.
Chinese official media has neither shared the names of the missing nor published much footage of the families' reactions.
But dozens of social media posts, reviewed by AFP, offer a glimpse into the emotional toll the catastrophe has taken.
"Hurry up and come back, your parents miss you a lot, we need you," one woman wrote on a  platform on Wednesday.
She attached a photo of a her relative — a police officer — and his wife, who are thought to have been at the Gyirong border post  when it was overwhelmed by a torrent of water, mud and debris that buried buildings and roads.
A previous post by the same woman showed a photo of a plane ticket to Tibet.
She told AFP  that she had not been able to reach the couple since the flood and had been told by her relative's work unit that he was missing.
Family members of the missing were being temporarily housed in the area, she said at the time.
She has since stopped replying to messages from AFP.
Chinese authorities tightly restrict access to Tibet for foreign journalists, and AFP knows of no overseas outlets that have been able to visit the disaster site there.
Officials and state media have focused on the scale of search operations, with some reports giving extensive space to the deployment of more than 2,300 rescuers along with helicopters and drones.
They have also highlighted the concern of the country's leaders. President Xi Jinping convened an emergency meeting on aid efforts, and Premier Li Qiang travelled to Tibet in the immediate aftermath.
As of a week after the floods, the death toll from inside China stood at 21, with 541 people missing.
In Nepal, the figures were more than 1,287 dead and over  5,000 missing as of  Friday.
Nearly 100 Chinese remain unaccounted for in Nepal, according to Beijing's Foreign Ministry.
Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely".
Local authorities were "promptly replying" to more than 800 calls from affected relatives, state news agency Xinhua reported on Wednesday.
Online, relatives of China's missing have written of going days without updates, and of travelling to Tibet to wait for news.
Border police, tourists and construction workers are among those unaccounted for on both sides of the border, the posts show.
"I hope a miracle will happen. We all miss you very much. You must not leave us behind," wrote one father about his daughter, another police officer at the border.
"My heart hurts so much, and I haven't been able to sleep at night," a wife wrote to her husband.
Another seemed resigned to the worst outcome: "You left so suddenly, leaving behind elderly parents and young children. What are we supposed to do?"
Users shared screenshots of the names of the missing released by Nepali authorities, which include people from China.
The article is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Rayer calls for probe into alleged Pas-US meeting
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: Jelutong member of parliament RSN Rayer has called for an investigation into an alleged meeting between Pas leaders and United States officials concerning efforts to topple the government.
Rayer said the allegation, reportedly revealed by
Pas president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang
at the party's muktamar, could not be dismissed as a political anecdote.
"If the allegation is accurate, this is not merely a matter of partisan politics. It is a matter of national security and national sovereignty," he said tonight.
Rayer said the public deserved to know who attended the alleged meeting, when and where it took place, who authorised it and what was discussed.
He also questioned whether any foreign government representative had been involved in attempts to influence, destabilise or facilitate the removal of the duly elected Malaysian government.
Rayer described the alleged failure to report such a meeting to Malaysian authorities as "treachery" and "treason".
He called on Abdul Hadi to explain why the alleged meeting was not immediately reported to the then prime minister, Home Ministry, Foreign Ministry, police or relevant national security agencies.
"Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy. We are a democratic sovereign state.
"Governments are changed through the ballot box and constitutional processes, not through secret meetings with foreign powers," he stressed.
Rayer urged the government, particularly the prime minister and relevant national security agencies, to investigate Abdul Hadi's claim.
He added that the issue should not be viewed through the political rivalry involving Pas, Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional or Perikatan Nasional.
"This is about Malaysia," he said, adding that no political party should engage a foreign government in discussions concerning the overthrow or destabilisation of Malaysia's elected government.
Rayer said Malaysia's sovereignty was "bigger than any political party" and no foreign power should be allowed to interfere in determining who governs the country.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: One year after founder's death, Armani needs to find a new fit
Article:
ONE year after the death of founder Giorgio Armani, the Italian fashion house is entering a pivotal period as the clock starts ticking on plans for an initial stake sale, after the group spent the last year focused on governance.
Armani, who died aged 91 on Sept 4, 2025, stipulated in his will that a first sale of around 15 per cent of the company should take place between 12 and 18 months after his death, followed by the disposal of a larger stake or a bourse listing.
Industry executives and analysts warn, however, that one year on, the late designer's heirs and advisers must now focus on evolving, to keep the brand fresh and relevant.
"Continuity is the right choice to get through the first year. It becomes, or could become, a risk if it turns into inertia," said Francesco Fiorese, a partner at consultancy Simon Kucher.
The real test for the company, Fiorese said, will be to switch from "a succession model based on Giorgio Armani's legacy to a more autonomous system, capable of making its own decisions while still preserving the brand's identity".
Over the last year, Armani's sales declined 2.8 per cent at constant currencies to €2.2 billion, and investors remain cautious about the luxury sector's health as the war with Iran drags on and Chinese consumer spending  falters.
As he prepares a new business plan, CEO Giuseppe Marsocci, a group veteran now at the helm, told an event in July that Armani would not seek short-term fixes, while keeping faithful to the founder's long-term vision of an essential and elegant style with attention to detail and wearability.
He said Armani was still in a transition phase and looking for a new balance as the founding family worked closely with new board directors, including former Gucci CEO Marco Bizzarri.
Marsocci pointed to a joint venture to develop new Armani Hotels & Resorts as an indication of future strategic moves.
"The great challenge will be maintaining the balance between the identity that defines us and the inevitable evolution we will have to pursue," he said.
In his will, Armani listed France's LVMH and licensees EssilorLuxottica and L'Oréal as potential buyers, or another luxury group of comparable standing.
The fashion house, which sources said is working with Rothschild as financial adviser for the sale, had €500 million in net cash at the end of 2025.
Two people close to the matter said there was no pressure to clinch a sale and the deadlines set out in Armani's will are not strictly binding.
The process is expected to accelerate in the coming weeks, but a deal could be postponed if market conditions fail to support an adequate valuation, the sources said.
Bankers and advisers consulted by Reuters put the group's valuation at €5 billion to €7 billion.
For L'Oreal and EssilorLuxottica, a stake in Armani would help to protect licensing deals which last year netted almost €2 billion in revenue for the groups — and royalties for Armani.
"Licensing deals with L'Oreal and EssilorLuxottica have been profitable.
"With the market demanding more accessible entry points, like accessories and beauty, as consumer spending tightens, these areas show strong potential for continued growth," said Gonzalo Brujó, CEO of consultancy Interbrand Global.
EssilorLuxottica would be interested only in a small holding and could consider partnering with other bidders, two people close to the matter said.
L'Oréal has little interest in entering the fashion business but is keen to safeguard a beauty licence that runs until 2050, according to another person close to the matter.
LVMH, large enough to incorporate fashion, eyewear and beauty, has  studied the possibility of a stand-alone investment, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter.
The writers are from Reuters

Title: Man suffers head, leg injuries after falling from tree
Article:
SEREMBAN: A 45-year-old man sustained head injuries and a fractured leg after falling from a tree while picking fruit at Gunung Berembun here this afternoon.
A Negri Sembilan Fire and Rescue Department spokesman said the department received an emergency call at 2.49pm.
"The victim was believed to be five kilometres from the Forestry Registration Post. Initial information from the caller indicated that the man had sustained head injuries and was unable to continue his journey down the hill.
"He was believed to be near the Gunung Berembun waterfall.
"Additional assistance from the Special Tactical Operation and Rescue Team was required as the victim was seriously injured after falling from a tree," the spokesman said.
The spokesman added that the victim was given initial treatment before being brought down to the foot of the hill.

Title: Jom Heboh gives Melaka businesses an economic boost
Article:
AYER KEROH: The Jom Heboh concert in Melaka is more than an entertainment event, with its large crowds helping to drive the local economy and benefiting small businesses and entrepreneurs.
Melaka Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh said large-scale events such as the concert could generate a ripple effect across the local economy, as visitors not only attended the performances but also spent at food outlets, shopped, stayed at hotels and used transport services.
He said this indirectly created more opportunities for small businesses and local operators to increase their income.
"I want every celebration we create to bring benefits back to the people," he said when speaking at the Jom Heboh Concert held in conjunction with the Karnival Anak Muda Melaka x Konsert Jom Heboh at the Melaka International Trade Centre (MITC) here tonight.
Also present were state secretary Datuk Salhah Salleh; state Tourism, Heritage, Arts and Culture Committee exco Datuk Abd Razak Abd Rahman; and Media Prima TV Networks' Group Editor for News and Current Affairs Datuk Azhari Muhiddin.
Ab Rauf thanked Media Prima Berhad, TV3 and the Jom Heboh team for bringing the event back to Melaka, and expressed hope that the media conglomerate would continue to choose the state as one of its main destinations for future editions.
Meanwhile, the two-day Karnival Anak Muda Melaka, which began yesterday, has attracted about 50,000 visitors.
Ab Rauf said the state government had provided various activities during the carnival, including e-sports, an AI Showcase, the Army Warrior Challenge, Muay Thai, Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), career and entrepreneurship programmes, as well as a town hall session.
"When we talk about young people, we cannot talk only about entertainment. They need opportunities to learn, work, do business, create and, most importantly, to be heard.
"That is why Karnival Anak Muda Melaka is not just a place for us to gather, but a platform for Melaka's youth, where talent can be discovered, ideas heard and opportunities opened up," he said.

Title: Sultanah Aminah Hospital launches probe into sexual harassment allegations involving specialist
Article:
JOHOR BARU: Sultanah Aminah Hospital (HSA) has launched an internal investigation into allegations of sexual harassment involving a medical specialist in the Department of Anaesthesiology.
The Johor Health Department, in a statement today, said the hospital management had established a special investigation committee to investigate the report, which was received on Aug 28.
It said the investigation followed a report by a portal alleging that certain parties had asked the complainant to withdraw the misconduct report concerning the sexual harassment allegations.
"The investigation is being completed before action is taken in accordance with the guidelines and procedures currently in place.
"The hospital will not tolerate any attempt to conceal, suppress, pressure or prevent any staff member from making a report concerning allegations of sexual harassment," the statement said.
The department said HSA remained committed to ensuring justice for all parties while upholding transparency and integrity throughout the investigation process.

Title: Jokowi calls on leaders, people to build peace through mutual understanding
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: Former Indonesian president Joko Widodo, popularly known as Jokowi, has called on leaders and the people to strengthen mutual understanding, saying it is the foundation for lasting peace.
Opening the Penang Peace Dialogue alongside Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow here tonight, Jokowi said leaders must understand and respond to the concerns and aspirations of their people.
"In times like this, the role of leaders becomes really important.
"A leader is not only someone who understands strategy and power, but someone who truly understands their people, who listens to them, feels their concerns, understands their problems and works for their future," he said.
However, he said responsibility for building peace did not rest with leaders alone, as the people must also understand the direction and challenges faced by their leaders.
Jokowi said a strong society was not one that merely made demands, but one that also understood the direction and challenges faced by its leaders.
Describing the dialogue as an opportunity to share ideas, learn from one another and work together for peace and a better future, he expressed hope that the gathering would lead to meaningful action.
Meanwhile, Chow said trust should be treated as essential infrastructure for cooperation, as it was crucial for countries to remain connected amid increasing strategic rivalry and diverging interests.
He said global connectivity had brought economic opportunities to Penang through its manufacturing, semiconductor and technology sectors, but also exposed economies to disruptions when divisions deepened across borders and supply chains.
"In a more multipolar world, trust must also become an infrastructure of cooperation. Connectivity can bring countries together, but trust is what allows them to remain together when interests begin to diverge," he said.
Chow said countries and societies did not need to agree on every issue, but they must understand differing interests, maintain open communication and identify areas where cooperation remained possible.
Themed 'Bridging Civilisations in a Multipolar World', the two-day dialogue is the centrepiece of the Commonwealth of World Chinatowns (CWC) Conference Series in Penang, bringing together about 200 delegates. Jokowi is scheduled to deliver his keynote address tomorrow.
The CWC is a project aimed at bringing Chinatowns around the world closer together, beginning with Penang and Singapore, while promoting exchanges beyond Chinese culture and traditions in areas such as art, culture, history, science, technology and research.
